newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia debt trounced, rate cut less likely.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia debt trounced, rate cut less likely.

text.p: *The Australian debt market succumbed to a hefty sell-off after the latest data on wages suggested that a further monetary policy easing was now less likely.
*Focus now on Friday's key U.S. non-farm payrolls data.
The Australian debt market succumbed to hefty sell-off after the latest data on wages growth came in at the top end of expectations.
Some analysts now believe a cut in the current 6.0 percent official interest rates is completely off the agenda.

"The latest wages data suggesting that the continuing moderation in wages growth over early 1996 stalled at around 4.0 percent in the second half of the year, reinforces our view that the RBA will not move again this cycle," said John Peters, senior economist at Westpac Banking Corp.
November quarter average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) rose 1.2 percent, bringing the annual growth rate to 3.9 percent and above the 3.8 percent in the August quarter.
Forecasts had centred on an annual rate of 3.6 percent.

The short-end of the market was the hardest hit having been holding out for at least a 25 basis points easing by early March even after the Reserve Bank left policy unchanged following last Tuesday's board meeting.
The March bill futures contract dropped to 94.13 at one stage, indicating a cash rate of 5.87 percent, while short-dated bond yields were up over 20 basis points.
However, some analysts believe there is still a possibility that the RBA could ease again.
"Bond markets are simply realising that another rate cut is not a foregone conclusion," said Matthew Drennan, senior economist at Axiom Funds Management.

However, "Any decision to cut rates further will depend on three factors - whether further fiscal tightening in the May budget will dent consumer and business confidence, the size of the increase granted under the ACTU's 'living wage' claim and the strength of the labour market," he added,
January labour force data is due next week.
The local yield curve flattened sharply on the data, while yield spreads to other bloc bonds widened.
Focus will switch to the U.S. market, which faces the key non-farm payrolls report on Friday, and as it adjusts in preparation for next week's quarterly refunding auctions.
